title: Matteo Ricci in China (1552–1610)
hookLine: a Jesuit who learned Chinese, dressed as a scholar and made friends

cards: An Italian with a long beard sits in a scholar's silk robe, in a city at the far end of the world from Rome. His guests haven't come for a sermon.

They've come for his maps, his clocks, his mathematics, and his memory, which could do tricks they had never seen. They argue with him about Confucius. He argues back, in their language, quoting their classics.
Some become his friends. A few become Christians. His name is Matteo Ricci, a Jesuit, and the long word for what he was trying to do is today's word.

teach.b: Inculturation means letting the faith take root in a culture, speaking its language and wearing its clothes, without stopping being itself. Ricci never used the word; it came much later.
But his life is one of the stories Catholics reach for to explain it. First, the language.

Ricci and his companions studied Chinese for years, spoken and written, until he could write books Chinese scholars read seriously. Second, the clothes. At first the Jesuits dressed like Buddhist monks.
Then Ricci noticed who was listening: the educated class who read Confucius.

teach.h: FROM MONK'S ROBE TO SCHOLAR'S ROBE.
teach.b: So he changed into a scholar's robes.
Third, friendship. One of his early books in Chinese was a small collection of sayings on friendship, drawn from Western writers. In effect it said: I came a long way, to be your friend.
One friend, the scholar Xu Guangqi, became a Christian and worked with him translating geometry. Fourth, the hard question.
Ricci judged that Chinese Christians could keep honoring Confucius and the ancestors as a civil and family custom, not worship. Others in the Church strongly disagreed.
The argument went on long after his death, and Church rulings on it changed over time. So inculturation isn't a slogan.
It's a question you keep asking: what belongs to the faith, and what is simply the coat it arrived in?
Paul put the instinct in one line, in the Douay-Rheims: "I became all things to all men, that I might save all."

how: Catholic missionaries and bishops speak of inculturation when they bring the liturgy, music and art of a local culture into the life of the Church, and Ricci is often remembered in that conversation, especially by Jesuits.

games.q: you're Ricci. Chinese friends who become Christians ask whether they may still honor Confucius and their ancestors. what do you judge?
o: they must give up every such custom.
these honors can be kept as civil and family custom, not worship.
leave it to each family and say nothing.
games.why: Ricci judged them civil and family custom. others in the Church disagreed strongly, and the argument outlived him.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose family comes from somewhere you don't, and notice where your knowing about their world stops: a food, a holiday, a word.
Pick one thing you'd like to ask them, not to study them, but because friends ask. If you pray, hold them before God; if not, hold them in mind with curiosity.

wordCard.voice: Inculturation. The faith taking root in a culture, in its language and its clothes, while staying itself. Matteo Ricci, in a scholar's robe, is a story Catholics tell about it.

carryVoice: Your line: friendship first. Ricci came a long way to be a friend before anything else. Day eight hundred fifty-seven, done.
